I ask you to include yourself. The Public Office (Accountability) Bill will make it a crime to mislead the public intentionally or recklessly if you are a minister, civil servant, police officer or soldier, or even in the intelligence services. Yet peers, MPs, MSPs, MSs and MLAs are carved out of their own law. Please vote to end this carve-out for lies they tell the public beyond their parliaments: at public events, on TV and radio, and on social media.

It does not matter whether you are a minister. Minister and legislator are two different roles, with two different capacities, and you must be prosecutable as a legislator as well as a minister: accountable under both.

Please do not reply with the Cabinet Office's prepared lines for MPs. ExecProsec, the campaign leading this petition, has examined them all, and none survives scrutiny, as shown below.

## 1. Privilege is no barrier
The Government says privilege protects words spoken in Parliament. That would not change: our amendment threatens nothing and respects privilege in full, as it covers only public statements outside parliament.

It goes further. The Senedd, the Scottish Parliament and the Northern Ireland Assembly lack parliamentary privilege, with only limited protection against slander claims, and the Bill as drafted grants no immunity from prosecution for anything said there. A government minister lying there could currently be prosecuted for misleading the public, which is a major oversight. Our amendment shields proceedings in every other UK parliament from prosecution for the new offences, which neither the Government nor the Bill has even considered.

## 2. Procedures are no barrier either
We are told Parliament regulates its own affairs. Yet its rules reach only what is said inside it, not lies told to the public outside. A jury decides when a civil servant or police officer lies to the public. MPs and peers should be treated alike.

## 3. Executive power is no test
Backbenchers and peers, the Government says, take no decisions for the state. They need not. They scrutinise the Government, vote on legislation and public spending, and shape decisions of national importance. Most are elected, trusted to report back on the Government's conduct, and must be trusted to tell the truth when they speak about it. In our system executive power means nothing without scrutiny from the backbenches and opposition. If ministers may be prosecuted for lying while shadow ministers and scrutinisers may not, checks and balances are thrown entirely off balance whenever legislators address the public.

## 4. Lying needs no secret information
Backbenchers and peers are also said to lack ministers' information. This entirely misunderstands lying. It does not rely on access to the truth; a lie is the opposite of the truth. It needs only a readiness to make things up.

## 5. An election is not a trial
Elected members, the Government says, answer to voters at elections. Elections, though, determine who holds office, and reflect how popular a party, leader or policy is. A prosecution asks something else: did one individual deliberately deceive the public? Only a jury, weighing the evidence carefully at trial, can settle that; no election can.

The expenses scandal shows this. Elected politicians were jailed for false expense claims: election did not put them above the law, and they faced justice, as everyone should. Peers never stand for election at all.

## 6. Political speech is safe, and Hillsborough is no limit
First, we are not trying to criminalise political speech. Our purpose is that ordinary political debate, opinions, broken promises and honest mistakes can never be prosecuted.

Second, nothing in the Bill confines it to cover-ups of the Hillsborough kind. It should certainly cover those, but equally a lie to start a war or to manipulate a referendum result. The threshold for conviction is high, yet the offence can rightly reach a very broad range of situations.

## Conclusion
Should Parliament vote to exempt its own members, it would leave me angry and betrayed. A law that binds everyone except those who make it is a law for thee, but not for me. Public trust in the UK's parliaments would be destroyed, as you would be telling us you wanted to stay free to lie to us.

It would show you have learnt nothing from years of lying in politics, endured from Iraq to the Brexit referendum and the scandals of the COVID-19 pandemic, and countless others. Politicians rank among the least trusted professions in the country for a reason. Do you seriously want to do this? For Parliament, it would be the most damaging and reputationally self-harming step imaginable.

Government ministers will look like heroes for including themselves, while the Government sets legislators up to look like traitors and people who consider themselves above the law. Being left out of this law is not protection from it but a humiliation.

The Lords vote on the amendment next. More peers have so far spoken for it than against, so the Lords seem likely to add it before it goes back to the Commons for final approval. Please tell me how you will vote then.

They scrutinise the Government, vote on public spending and laws, and influence decisions of national importance. This would prove that, after years of lies in politics endured over Iraq, the Brexit referendum, the scandals of the COVID-19 pandemic and countless others, you have still not learnt your lesson. It is no accident that politicians are among the country's least trusted professions. Do you seriously want to do this? Nothing could do Parliament more damage, or be more reputationally self-harming.

Next, the House of Lords votes on the amendment. Up to now, more peers have spoken in its favour than against it, so the Lords look likely to add it, and then the Commons gives final approval. Please tell me how you will vote when that happens.
